utterances.text: Welcome to Miss Marjoribanks Unpacked — a close, unhurried, and genuinely affectionate look at one of the most dazzling comic novels of the Victorian era.
Miss Marjoribanks, published in 1866 by Mrs Oliphant, follows Lucilla Marjoribanks — a young woman of formidable intelligence, total self-possession, and quite breathtaking social ambition.
She returns from school to her widower father's provincial town, and proceeds — calmly, methodically, brilliantly — to reorganise its entire social life around herself.

The novel is a masterwork of irony, of social comedy, and of something far harder to name — a genuine investigation of what intelligence and energy look like when they have nowhere large enough to go.
To explore it with me today, I have three guests who bring wonderfully different lights to bear on Oliphant's work.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than almost anyone alive.
He comes to every novel as a performer first — alert to rhythm, to comic timing, to the sentences that were written for the voice rather than the silent page.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong Tory who believes a novelist's genius lies in moral imagination — in stories about character tested by circumstance.
He is beautifully spoken, deeply well-read, and not easily impressed — which makes his enthusiasm, when it comes, all the more worth having.
And Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — who asks, always, who benefits and who pays.
He earns his arguments with evidence, and he has a gift for finding the novel's sharpest edges precisely where you least expect them.
Let's begin, as the novel does, with Lucilla herself — who she is, how she works, and why she is so extraordinarily difficult to look away from.
The first thing I want to say about Lucilla Marjoribanks is that she is one of the great comic creations of the English novel — and I mean that without qualification.
What Oliphant gives her is not vanity — it's something far more interesting than vanity.
It is complete, serene, unshakeable conviction.
There's a passage very early on where Oliphant describes Lucilla's relationship to self-promotion — and it is one of the funniest and most precise things I have ever read.

"Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to her audience as well as to herself."
And then Oliphant adds — with beautiful economy — "Such a conviction is never without its fruits."
That last line is devastating — and perfectly timed.
The joke is that Lucilla's self-belief is not delusional — it actually works.
Oliver puts his finger on something important there — the distinction between vanity and conviction is not merely comic, it is morally significant.
Vanity is self-deception. Conviction — particularly Lucilla's variety — is a form of will.
And the question the novel poses, with remarkable seriousness beneath all its comedy, is whether that will is put to good use.
Oliphant is not satirising Lucilla's energy — she is examining it.
That is a rather different thing, and it is why the novel sustains interest long after the comedy of a lesser book would have exhausted itself.
I agree entirely about that distinction — but I want to press on what "its fruits" actually means in this novel.
Lucilla's conviction works because she operates in a social world that is already structured to reward precisely her kind of performance.
She has leisure, she has a house, she has a father with a comfortable income.
The conviction is not free-floating — it is materially grounded.
And Oliphant knows this — which is why the comedy has that slight chill underneath it that Oliver is pointing to.
That chill is exactly right — and it comes out most brilliantly, I think, in the passage where Oliphant describes Lucilla's return to Carlingford.
The narrator uses this extraordinary rhetoric — the language of revolution, of a transformative figure arriving to change everything.
And you expect — because the form seems to demand it — a great man.
"To be sure, it was not a man this time, but Miss Marjoribanks; but the atmosphere thrilled and trembled to the advent of the new luminary all the same."
"All the same" — those two words do all the work.
Oliphant is simultaneously mocking the grandiose language and absolutely meaning it.
Lucilla is a luminary. The joke doesn't cancel the claim — it is the claim.
That formal irony — using the language of great historical arrival for a young woman with social ambitions in a provincial town — is one of Oliphant's most distinctive signatures.
But I would resist reading it as merely deflating.
The comedy works in both directions: it elevates Carlingford's drawing rooms into a theatre of genuine consequence, just as it reduces the rhetoric of revolution to something manageable.
Oliphant takes the domestic sphere seriously. That is not a comic concession — it is a considered moral position.
The domestic sphere is taken seriously — absolutely — but we should ask what that sphere costs to maintain, and who maintains it.
What I find compelling is the passage where Lucilla hears the contralto voice from the street.

"Who could it be that possessed that voice which Miss Marjoribanks felt by instinct was the very one thing wanting — a round, full, delicious contralto, precisely adapted to supplement without supplanting her own high-pitched and much-cultivated organ?"
That phrase — "supplement without supplanting" — is Lucilla's entire social philosophy in four words.
She recruits people. She incorporates them into a structure that serves her project.
The other woman's voice is heard first as an asset — a resource to be deployed.
That is not cruelty — Oliphant doesn't make it cruelty — but it tells us everything about the social logic Lucilla inhabits and enforces.
"Supplement without supplanting" — I've been performing this novel for years and that phrase still makes me want to applaud.
Because it reveals that Lucilla's generosity and Lucilla's self-interest are genuinely indistinguishable — even to Lucilla.
She is not calculating in any cold sense. She is calculating the way a great conductor is calculating — always in service of the whole performance.
And the performance, it turns out, is Carlingford itself — with Lucilla as both composer and first violin.
Lucilla as composer and first violin — a perfect image to carry into the next part of our conversation.
Because any great performance requires a stage — and Carlingford's social world is both the instrument Lucilla plays and the structure that makes her playing possible.
Next, we turn to the architecture of that social world — its classes, its hierarchies, and the very particular way power moves through the drawing rooms of Carlingford.

segments.title: The Architecture of Society: Class and Influence in Miss Marjoribanks

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Lucilla constructs herself as the centre of Carlingford's social world.
But the question this segment presses on is: what kind of architecture is she actually building — and who does it serve?
What strikes me most, reading these early chapters, is how precisely Oliphant maps the geography of power.
The Doctor's house isn't merely a setting — it's a military installation.
Listen to how the narrator describes it:
"Dr Marjoribanks's house could not have been better placed as a strategic position, commanding as it did all Grange Lane, of which it was, so to speak, the key."
Strategic position. Commanding. Key.
Oliphant is writing military geography — and she means it.
The house commands Grange Lane — the elite enclave — but it also provides access to, in the narrator's phrase, the profaner public.
Lucilla understands that consolidating a ruling class requires the periodic appearance of openness — and this position gives her exactly that leverage.
I don't dispute the spatial observation — it's sharp — but I think the word 'leverage' rather flattens what Oliphant is doing.
Lucilla's mastery of position is not purely instrumental — it is also a form of competence, of craft, which Oliphant genuinely admires.
The narrator is satirical, yes — but the satire contains something warmer than critique.
Consider what Oliphant tells us about Lucilla's method of expansion.
"Miss Marjoribanks prepared to establish her kingdom with a benevolence which was almost Utopian, not upon the ruins of other thrones, but with the goodwill and co-operation of the lesser powers."
Not upon the ruins of other thrones — that is a genuinely admirable political instinct, whatever one thinks of its ultimate ambitions.
She doesn't annihilate rivals — she incorporates them.
That is closer to good governance than to mere manipulation.
Edmund, I love that you've given Lucilla a Burkean constitution — and she would absolutely approve of the comparison.
But what delights me as a reader — as a performer of this text — is the sting in that qualifier: almost Utopian.
Oliphant is holding two things at once — genuine appreciation and very dry amusement.
And then she delivers the real blade: those lesser powers were, quote, too feeble to resist her advance.
The goodwill being co-operated is not entirely voluntary — and Oliphant knows it, and she's winking at us the whole time.
Oliver has it exactly right on that wink — and it connects directly to something Oliphant spells out even more bluntly earlier in the novel.
Lucilla understands something that most social comedies prefer to leave unspoken: women's influence in provincial society depends entirely on capturing men's attendance.
Oliphant lays the structural condition bare:

"In the very best society of a country town, husbands are very commonly unmanageable, and have a great deal more of their own way in respect to the houses they will or will not go to, than is good for that inferior branch of the human family."
That phrase — inferior branch of the human family — is delivered with such serene irony that it almost disarms you.
But Oliphant is telling us something real about the structural subordination of women's social labour — it must work through men, who retain the power of refusal.
Lucilla's genius is that she has studied this constraint and designed her entire campaign around it.
I would push back slightly on the word 'subordination,' though I take the point about constraint.
What Oliphant is also describing — with that magnificent phrase about a woman's right to be arbitrary — is a form of genuine power.
The passage reads: a brilliant position gives a woman a right to be arbitrary, and to select her materials according to her judgment.
That is not the language of a victim of structure — that is the language of a sovereign exercising discretion.
And what a sovereign she is when she turns that gaze inward on herself.
There's a passage I keep returning to — it's almost unbearably funny and yet oddly moving at the same time.
After a moment of doubt about whether she is truly understood:
"Lucilla passed through one of those moments of sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the benefactors of their race."
Benefactors of their race.
She has placed herself in the company of Napoleon, of Gladstone, of — I don't know — Prometheus.
And Oliphant gives her those tears — a few tears came to her eyes — with complete tenderness.
She is mocking Lucilla and loving her in the same breath — and that is extraordinarily hard to do.
That tenderness is real — but it shouldn't obscure what's being said about the cost of Lucilla's vision.
There's a passage where the narrator describes what sets Lucilla apart from everyone else in the room on one of her Thursday evenings.

"While every one else regarded the matter with, to some extent, a personal bias — the only person who looked at it abstractly, and contemplated not the accidents of an evening, but the work itself, which was progressing in the face of all kinds of social difficulties, was the master-mind which first conceived the grand design of turning the chaotic elements of society in Carlingford into one grand unity."
The master-mind. The grand design.
Oliphant is clear that what Lucilla sees is unity — but unity on whose terms, and at what cost to the chaotic elements she is busy organising?
The social difficulties she faces are the friction of people who don't fit the pattern she's designed.
And the novel will eventually ask whether the pattern is actually for them — or merely of them.
That is finely put — and I think the novel is alert to it.
But one should note that Lucilla's project is not simply self-aggrandisement — she genuinely believes in the value of the order she is creating.
The sublime despondency that Oliver so wonderfully read is not vanity alone — it is the loneliness of someone who sees a larger picture than those around her.
Oliphant may be ironic — she is always ironic — but she also grants Lucilla the dignity of genuine vocation.
Genuine vocation — and yet the world she has so carefully arranged is about to be disrupted in ways she cannot fully control.
Coming up: the Cavendish affair — and what happens when a very well-organised society encounters a scandal it simply cannot absorb.

segments.title: Scandal and Structure: The Cavendish Affair Unravels

utterances.text: We've been examining how Carlingford's social architecture rewards certain performances of class and belonging.
Now we need to look at what happens when that performance is exposed — when the scaffolding gives way.
The Cavendish affair is the novel's great structural crisis — a scandal that tests every power relation in Carlingford simultaneously.
What strikes me most about Oliphant's handling of Cavendish is how entirely the drama turns on identity — not morality, not money, but name.
There is a passage that cuts straight to the heart of it.

"he could rather be content to lose them all at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not, after all, one of the Cavendishes"
Financial ruin he could survive — social counterfeit he could not.
That is a precise and rather devastating observation about what Victorian society actually valued.
Edmund is right, and I'd push it a step further.
What Cavendish fears isn't exposure of a lie — it's expulsion from the class whose legitimacy is entirely constructed.
The name 'Cavendish' is a social credential — it carries access, deference, political candidacy.
And the novel is ruthlessly clear about what that credential buys.
Look at the passage describing him going out to face his crisis — Oliphant strips the whole enterprise bare.
"In this battle no honour, but only a possible salvage of reputation and fortunate escape, was to be gained."
No honour — only salvage. That's the vocabulary of wreckage, not of gentlemanly contest.
The thing I keep coming back to, as a performer, is Lucilla's face during all of this.
She already knows. And Oliphant gives us that knowledge through what is absent from her expression.
Here's the passage — and it's a masterclass in how to write a character who holds all the cards:
"Lucilla regarded him through all these fluctuations with natural pity, and at the same time with the calmness of a knowledge which was aware of all and had nothing more to discover"

"and at the end Mr Cavendish perceived her calm, and the absence of wonder and curiosity in her face, and began to perceive that he had something very serious to deal with — more serious even than he had at first supposed."
It's the absence of surprise that terrifies him. That's the whole comedy and the whole menace of Lucilla in one stroke.
And then comes the scene that Oliphant has been building toward — the moment of revelation at table, with the Archdeacon.
It is rendered with a kind of gothic precision that is quite unlike Oliphant's usual tone.
"he looked, and he saw at the centre of the table, surrounded by every kind of regard and consideration, full in the light of the lamp, his favourite adventurer, the impostor whom he had denounced"
That phrase — 'full in the light of the lamp' — is doing tremendous visual work.
Cavendish is positioned at the very heart of Lucilla's social world, honoured, at the moment he is about to be unmasked.
And then — and this is where Oliphant is almost wickedly funny — the Archdeacon overplays his hand.
He goes too far in his accusation, and it's that excess that saves Cavendish.
Listen to how Oliphant stages this reversal:
"A criminal? a conspirator? said Mr Cavendish, and he looked in his accuser's face with an amazement which, notwithstanding his rage, struck the Archdeacon."
"If he had called him an impostor, the culprit would have quailed and made no reply. But the exaggeration saved him."
Genuine shock at a false charge — that's a comedy of legal hair-splitting that a barrister would appreciate.
What this exposes structurally is that the accusation of social fraud is almost unutterable in polite society.
You can call a man a criminal — a lurid, concrete charge — but to say he is not who he claims to be touches something more foundational.
The social order depends on that kind of identity claim going unchallenged.
And then Oliphant extends the irony brilliantly into the election chapters.
After everything — the scandal, the near-exposure, the months away — Cavendish walks straight back into Barbara Lake's parlour on the eve of the election.
Oliphant's summary of this is almost a legal indictment in rhythm:
"He was there — he who had been so long away from Carlingford — he who had been so deeply offended by hearing his name seriously coupled with that of Barbara Lake"
"— he who ought to have been anywhere in the world rather than here upon the eve of his election, when all the world was keeping watch over his conduct."
Three anaphoric clauses — each one tightening the noose — and then the narrator simply drops him into the room. It's devastating.
And fate, with perfect economy, places his Dissenting supporters on the doorstep as he leaves.
Oliphant's sense of timing here is almost musical.
"When he was coming out of the house, as a matter of course, he met with the chief of his Dissenting supporters"
"both of whom stopped with a curiously critical air to speak to the Candidate, who had to be every man's friend for the time being."
'As a matter of course.' That parenthetical shrug from the narrator is the whole joke.
Of course they were there. Of course. Cavendish cannot take a step without the world arranging itself to witness it.
That phrase 'every man's friend for the time being' is one of Oliphant's quiet masterstrokes.
'For the time being.' Three words that contain an entire political career.
What I find so pleasurable about this whole sequence is that Cavendish is not a villain — he's a particular kind of weak man that Oliphant knows intimately.
He's self-deceiving, vain, constitutionally unable to resist what he knows will destroy him.
Oliphant writes him with pity and with comedy in the same breath — which is, of course, the more severe judgment.
What's remarkable is that Oliphant never needs melodrama to expose him — the social machinery does the work with perfect, almost gleeful efficiency.
And that efficiency — that comic precision in the way judgment is delivered — is exactly what we want to turn to next.
We'll be looking at Oliphant's wit as an instrument — how humour in this novel is never merely decorative, but does the sharpest social work of all.

segments.title: Wit as Weapon: Oliphant's Comic Voice and Social Power

utterances.text: We've been following the unravelling of the Cavendish affair — the social tremors it sent through Carlingford.
What I want to turn to now is the instrument Oliphant uses to register all that social pressure — her comic voice, and the remarkable women who wield it.
Oliver, Mrs Woodburn is your territory — a woman whose entire social power rests on the ability to become other people.
She is one of the most extraordinary minor characters in Victorian fiction, and I say that without any hesitation whatsoever.
The mimic is a figure who vanishes into other people — and yet, paradoxically, is never more herself than in that moment of disappearance.
And the passage where Mrs Woodburn's talent reaches its absolute peak — Oliphant calls it an apotheosis, which is exactly the right word — is one of the funniest things in the book.
"She shook off her languor as by a sudden inspiration, and gave such a sketch of the Archdeacon as up to this day is remembered more clearly in Carlingford than the man himself."
The man himself — outranked by his own impression.
That is a joke, but it is also a genuine and rather devastating observation about what performance does to reality.
I think what arrests me there is the word 'languor' — it appears repeatedly in connection with Mrs Woodburn.
She is indolent by disposition, and only the exercise of her peculiar gift rouses her to real effort.
Oliphant is making a moral point dressed in comic clothing.
Talent without perseverance, however brilliant, remains essentially passive — even parasitic.
And Lucilla, by contrast, has what Oliphant calls — with considerable admiration — 'the steady force, the persevering energy — or, to sum up all in one word, the genius — of Miss Marjoribanks.'
Genius, in Oliphant's moral vocabulary, is not a gift — it is an exercise of will.
I take Edmund's point, but I want to press on what the labour of entertainment actually means in Carlingford.
Mrs Woodburn's talent is a form of production — she generates social value, she holds the room together, she makes the evening work.
And yet she receives no material return, no institutional recognition — she is useful to Lucilla's project, deployed as an instrument.
The narrator tells us as much directly — Lucilla 'recognised the use of such an instrument of entertainment as Mrs Woodburn possessed.'
An instrument — that is not the language of friendship or admiration.
That is the language of management, of consciously organised social power.
Daniel is right that 'instrument' is doing extraordinary work there — but I want to add one thing, because Oliphant's comedy cuts in more than one direction at once.
The joke about Lucilla having no sense of humour is itself the sharpest joke in the chapter.
Listen to how Oliphant phrases it — and the phrasing is everything.
"Lucilla had no sense of humour, as she candidly admitted, with that consciousness of her own faults, and slight disposition to consider them virtues, which is common to persons of great endowments."
'Slight disposition to consider them virtues' — that is a sentence that takes you three readings to fully appreciate.
Lucilla knows her faults — but only just enough to feel rather proud of them.
That is Oliphant at her most precise — the irony is not savage, it is affectionate, but it is irony nonetheless.
She admires Lucilla, one feels that throughout — and yet she will not let her off the hook entirely.
A novelist without that quality — without the capacity to hold admiration and gentle mockery simultaneously — would have made Lucilla merely heroic, and entirely unreadable.
I want to bring in a passage that seems farcical on the surface but repays very close attention.
A barrister in Carlingford is describing the prospect of a public hanging — and this is the register he uses.
"It's a famous amusement for a country town."
An execution — a famous amusement.
The barrister goes on to describe the memorials, the insanity defences, the crowds of criminals descending on Carlingford — all with the breezy tone of a man planning a garden party.
Oliphant is using comic voice here to expose something genuinely brutal about the society she is describing — its complete ease with violence as spectacle.
That is a beautifully uncomfortable passage to read aloud — because the barrister is funny, and you laugh, and then you hear what you've just laughed at.
It's the same technique at work in the Archdeacon scene — comedy as a kind of sleight of hand.
Mrs Woodburn takes the Archdeacon off to his very face — and he never knows.
"She took him off to his very face, and he never found it out, though everybody else did, and the house shook with restrained laughter."
'Restrained laughter' — that is the entire novel in two words.
Carlingford is always restraining itself — barely, and only just, and with enormous effort.
Restrained laughter — and restrained virtue too, perhaps.
Because underpinning all of Oliphant's comedy is a serious ethical argument — about what people owe each other, and what the good life actually looks like in a provincial drawing room.
That's precisely where we're heading next — the moral depth beneath the wit.

segments.title: Moral Depth and Domestic Virtue: The Novel's Ethical Argument

utterances.text: We've been tracing how Oliphant's comedy functions as a kind of social X-ray — wit as diagnosis.
But underneath that satirical surface, there's a sustained ethical argument — about what it means to be good, to persist, to lead.
And this is precisely where the novel demands to be taken seriously as moral fiction, not merely as social comedy.
What Oliphant is tracing in Lucilla is something the eighteenth century would have recognised immediately — character under pressure.
There is a passage that strikes me as one of the most quietly remarkable in the novel.
"Her instinct, even when reason suggested that she should be doubtful of them, was always to side with her own friends."

Oliphant continues: "though there might be persons included in that sacred number who were scarcely worthy of the character, yet Lucilla, like every lofty character, could act but according to her own nature."
Now that phrase — 'like every lofty character, could act but according to her own nature' — is not satire.
It is a genuine claim about the integrity of the virtuous will.
I want to push back on that — gently — because 'acting according to one's nature' is also exactly what an ideology of class tells people to do.
The 'lofty character' who cannot forsake her own — that's a portrait of a ruling sensibility naturalising its own authority.
Lucilla's loyalty is real, I grant that.
But notice who benefits from it — always those within her social circle, her 'sacred number,' as Oliphant calls it.
The virtue is real; the scope of that virtue is class-bounded.
That is a sharp observation, and I won't entirely dismiss it.
But I think it mistakes a circumscribed virtue for a corrupted one.
Lucilla's fidelity, whatever its limits, is absolutely genuine — and genuine fidelity of any kind is morally significant.
Can I come at this from a different angle — because what I find most extraordinary is what Oliphant does with ingratitude.
There is a passage in Chapter Twenty-Seven that stops you cold.
"The idea of giving them up, and leaving their affairs to their own guidance, never for an instant penetrated into her heroic mind."
"But she was human, and naturally she felt the prick of ingratitude."
'The prick of ingratitude' — that is a novelist working at the absolute top of her range.
One word — 'prick' — and you have the whole thing: the dignity held intact, and underneath it, the small sharp wound.
And 'heroic mind' is not irony — or not only irony.
I agree completely about the prose — Oliver is right that something genuinely moving is happening there.
But what I want to ask is: who are 'her subjects' whose ingratitude stings her?
They are people she manages, organises, improves — people whose social lives are raw material for her campaigns.
The novel acknowledges the 'prick' of ingratitude, as Oliver says — but it never questions whether the benevolence was asked for.
Now here the novel's own ambiguity is, I think, its greatest strength.
Oliphant does not resolve the tension between Lucilla's genuine heroism and her rather formidable self-possession.
And Chapter Thirty-Six gives us perhaps the most direct statement of what Oliphant believes about her heroine.
"But as for Miss Marjoribanks, she stood bravely at her post, and scorned to flinch or run away."
"Thus commenced, amid mists of discouragement, and in an entire absence of all that was calculated to stimulate and exhilarate, the second grand period of Lucilla's life."
'Mists of discouragement' — without support, without applause — and she simply carries on.
That is not the behaviour of a social climber. That is the behaviour of someone who has internalised a calling.
The contrast Oliphant sets up at the beginning of that passage is beautifully sly, though.
She lists all the escape routes available to disappointed women: marriage tours, foreign travel, going out as a governess.
'People who know no better' — those are her words — may do those things.
The comedy is unmistakable — and yet the courage being praised is completely real.
I want to come back to the question of calling — because Oliphant is more honest about its limits than Edmund is suggesting.
There's a passage in Chapter Forty-Six where the narrator is quite direct about what Lucilla lacks.
She had 'no vocation, such as the foundress of such an establishment ought to have, nor did she see her way to the abandonment of all projects for herself.'

And then comes the sentence I find most arresting: "when a woman happens to be full of energy and spirit, and determined that whatever she may be she shall certainly not be a nonentity, her position is one that demands thought."
'Not a nonentity' — that's the minimum condition, and it's still in 1866 a radical demand for a woman to make.
The 'position that demands thought' is precisely what the novel is thinking through — without resolving it.
On that point, I find myself in complete agreement with Daniel — which is not a position I occupy with any regularity.
The novel's ethical seriousness lies precisely in this refusal to offer Lucilla a comfortable resolution.
She is not sanctified. She is not satirised out of existence.
She is held — rather as the great moralists hold difficult figures — in a state of productive, unresolved complexity.
Energy, loyalty, the prick of ingratitude, the refusal to be a nonentity — these are the coordinates of a character unlike almost any other in Victorian fiction.
And just when that character seems most alone in her second campaign, the novel sends someone back to her — someone who has been away a very long time.
We've been tracing the novel's moral architecture — the way Oliphant builds her ethical argument through domestic action and quiet virtue.
Now that framework gets tested by something rawer: the return of Tom Marjoribanks, and what his homecoming reveals about Lucilla's heart.
Tom's arc is one of the most quietly radical things in this novel, and I think it's easy to miss precisely because it's handled so lightly.
He's dispatched to India — effectively exiled — because Lucilla cannot yet accommodate what he represents emotionally.
And yet even in his absence, even when Lucilla has organised her entire social world without him, he haunts the novel.
Oliphant gives us this extraordinary observation about Lucilla's genius and its limits.
"She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple, unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla's heart when she said 'Poor Tom!'"
That word — comfort — is doing enormous work.
Genius, Oliphant tells us, can find its deepest relief not in an equal but in someone simply, honestly devoted to it.
That passage is almost a theorem, isn't it — stated with the calm authority of a mathematician proving something you felt but couldn't articulate.
But what I love is that Oliphant doesn't sentimentalise it.
She's clear-eyed: Lucilla is the genius, Tom is the simple unlucky fellow.
And then Tom comes back — and this is where Oliphant earns every bit of her craft — physically transformed.
Lucilla goes to welcome him with outstretched hands, perfectly composed, as she always is.

"She found herself, before she knew how, in the arms of a man with a beard, who was so much changed in his own person that he ventured to kiss her, which was a thing Tom Marjoribanks, though her cousin, had never dared to do before."
The beard!
The beard is the whole chapter in miniature — absence has changed him, hardened him, made him bold enough to act where once he only yearned.
Oliver puts it very well, though I'd frame the transformation slightly differently.
Tom has not merely grown bolder — he has grown worthy.
India is the crucible, in the old sense of the word — it has tested him, burned away the boyish want, and returned something more substantial.
And what strikes me as morally significant is what he says when he returns.
"There never was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if you had told me; and I have done it as near as possible."
That is not the language of passion overmastering reason.
That is the language of a man who has subordinated himself — freely, knowingly — to the person he loves most.
Oliphant is showing us that devotion, properly understood, is not weakness but a form of moral strength.
I'd push back on the word 'freely,' Edmund, because Tom's original departure was hardly a free choice.
He was, in the most practical sense, removed — sent to the colonies because he couldn't be accommodated at home.
That said, I think what Oliphant does with his return is genuinely surprising — and I mean that as praise.
She doesn't give us a triumphant lover claiming his reward.
She gives us Lucilla weeping — and the tears are not simple.
Oliphant writes that Lucilla cried abundantly —
"partly for grief, and partly because of the flutter of agitation, and something like joy."
Something like joy — not joy itself.
Oliphant is honest enough to keep a little ambiguity alive even in what should be the novel's most emotionally legible moment.
That phrase is the key to reading Lucilla throughout the whole novel, I think.
She is always feeling something like the thing she's supposed to feel — always slightly beside her own emotions, managing them even as she experiences them.
And what Tom's homecoming does — what the beard does, really — is finally catch her off guard.
Before she knew how — that's the phrase Oliphant uses.
Lucilla, who always knows how, suddenly doesn't — and that is the scene's entire emotional triumph.
And I think that is precisely where the novel's moral imagination is most acute.
Lucilla has spent ten years being entirely sufficient unto herself — her own architect, her own engine.
What Tom's return demonstrates is that sufficiency of that kind has a cost — a kind of loneliness that Lucilla herself has not quite named.
And Tom — simple, unlucky Tom — is the one who names it for her, simply by showing up.

Tom's homecoming, then, is where Oliphant's domesticity finally opens onto something the novel has been quietly withholding: the possibility that Lucilla's genius needs an object beyond Carlingford itself.
Which brings us, perhaps inevitably, to the question of what Lucilla's world ultimately cannot contain — and what that limitation means for the novel's legacy.

segments.title: Closing: The Limits and Legacies of Lucilla's World

utterances.text: We've been tracing the arc of Tom's return and what it costs Lucilla to accept a future she hadn't quite designed for herself.
That brings us, inevitably, to the largest question this novel poses: what do we make of Lucilla Marjoribanks — her genius, her limits, her strange kind of freedom?
What I keep coming back to is the way Oliphant refuses to let us pin Lucilla down with a simple motive.
There's a passage early in the novel where the narrator practically dares the cynical reader to reduce her.

"People who like to discover the alloy which blends with all human motives, may suppose that Lucilla felt her own credit as the leader of society at stake, and would not admit that she had been duped."
"But this had in reality but a very small share in the matter."
That "but a very small share" — delivered with such perfect composure — is Oliphant at her most wicked.
She's not exonerating Lucilla — she's saying the alloy is there, but it's simply not the main ingredient.
That's a far more interesting moral portrait than mere satire would permit.
Oliver has put his finger on something absolutely central to the moral intelligence of this novel.
Oliphant is not writing a fable about vanity punished, nor a polemic about female ambition thwarted.
She is writing about what it costs a person of genuine gifts to operate in a world that will not quite accommodate those gifts.
And the moral texture is all in that refusal to collapse Lucilla into a type.
She is not Becky Sharp — she is not Dorothea Brooke.
She is entirely, stubbornly, herself — which is the highest compliment one can pay a novelist's creation.
I want to press on this question of what Lucilla's gifts actually amount to — and at what cost they're exercised.
Because Oliphant is brutally clear-eyed about the structural irony of Lucilla's situation.
Listen to how the narrator sums up the arc of Lucilla's entire campaign in Carlingford.

"Miss Marjoribanks, like all other benefactors of their kind, had many sacrifices to make, and had to undergo the mortification of finding out that many of her most able efforts turned to other people's profit and went directly against herself."
"Turned to other people's profit and went directly against herself."
That is not merely the pathos of one woman's life — that is the logic of a system that extracts value from capable people and redistributes it upward.
Lucilla organises. Others profit. The novel is honest enough to name that plainly.
And yet — and this is the delicious paradox — Lucilla herself would not accept that framing for a single moment.
Because Oliphant also gives us this quite extraordinary description of Lucilla's inner life — her sense of her own enterprise.

"The enterprise might not be free from a touch of human vanity, but it was vanity of a loftier description: the pleasure of exercising a great faculty, and the natural confidence of genius in its own powers."
"Vanity of a loftier description." Oliphant wrote that completely straight-faced, and I love her for it.
Because it's also — genuinely — true. Lucilla's vanity really is of a loftier description than the vanity around her.
That phrase — "the natural confidence of genius in its own powers" — is one I find myself returning to.
Oliphant is not being ironic there — or rather, she is being ironic and entirely serious at the same time.
That double register — the satirical surface and the genuine respect beneath it — is precisely what separates Oliphant from a lesser novelist.
A lesser novelist would have punished Lucilla more completely, or celebrated her more sentimentally.
Oliphant does neither. She simply — observes. And in that observation lies the whole moral richness of the book.
I'd add only this: that the legacy of the novel is precisely its refusal to resolve the tension it has so carefully built.
Lucilla ends the novel with Tom, with Carlingford, with a life that looks — from the outside — like triumph.
But the narrator has shown us, clearly and without sentimentality, what that triumph has cost and who it has served.
That is not a comfortable ending. It is an honest one. And great novels earn their honesty.
That feels like exactly the right note to end on — honesty, earned over the full length of a remarkable novel.

We've ranged today across Lucilla's genius and her sacrifices, the social machinery she both masters and is mastered by, and the strange double register of Oliphant's narration — satirical and tender at once.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, to Sir Edmund Leigh, and to Daniel Rosen — three readers whose company makes any novel richer.
And to you, listening — thank you for spending this time with Miss Marjoribanks, a novel that has waited too long for the attention it deserves.

c2:p15.text:
There are people who talk of
themselves, and think of themselves, as it were, under protest, and with
depreciation, not actually able to convince themselves that anybody
cares; but Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound
conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and
clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to
her audience as well as to herself. Such a conviction is never without
its fruits.
c2:p15.summary: Lucilla's complete conviction in her own importance is the source of her persuasiveness; she genuinely believes her interests are everyone's interests.
c2:p15.best_quote: Lucilla, for her part, had the calmest and most profound conviction that, when she discussed her own doings and plans and clevernesses, she was bringing forward the subject most interesting to her audience as well as to herself

c3:p18.text:
To be
sure, it was not a man this time, but Miss Marjoribanks; but the
atmosphere thrilled and trembled to the advent of the new luminary all
the same.
c3:p18.summary: The narrator playfully reveals that the awaited transformative figure is not a man but Lucilla Marjoribanks, deflating grandiose revolutionary language through comic irony.
c3:p18.best_quote: To be sure, it was not a man this time, but Miss Marjoribanks; but the atmosphere thrilled and trembled to the advent of the new luminary all the same.

c4:p72.text:
Who could it be that possessed that voice
which Miss Marjoribanks felt by instinct was the very one thing
wanting—a round, full, delicious contralto, precisely adapted to
supplement without supplanting her own high-pitched and much-cultivated
organ? She stopped short before the door and made a rapid observation
even in the first moment of her surprise. The house was not exactly like
the other humble houses in Grove Street.
c4:p72.summary: Lucilla instinctively recognizes that this contralto voice is the perfect complement to her own soprano; it is the missing element for her social ambitions.
c4:p72.best_quote: Who could it be that possessed that voice which Miss Marjoribanks felt by instinct was the very one thing wanting—a round, full, delicious contralto, precisely adapted to supplement without supplanting her own high-pitched and much-cultivated organ?

c4:p64.text:
Dr
Marjoribanks's house could not have been better placed as a strategic
position, commanding as it did all Grange Lane, of which it was, so to
speak, the key, and yet affording a base of communication with the
profaner public, which Miss Marjoribanks was wise enough to know a
leader of society should never ignore completely; for, indeed, one of
the great advantages of that brilliant position is, that it gives a
woman a right to be arbitrary, and to select her materials according to
her judgment.
c4:p64.summary: The narrator observes that the Doctor's house commands Grange Lane geographically and socially, giving Lucilla strategic access to both elite and public society.
c4:p64.best_quote: Dr Marjoribanks's house could not have been better placed as a strategic position, commanding as it did all Grange Lane, of which it was, so to speak, the key

c10:p20.text:
"And she has a nice little voice," Lucilla said to
herself, with the most friendly and tolerant feelings. Thus Miss
Marjoribanks prepared to establish her kingdom with a benevolence which
was almost Utopian, not upon the ruins of other thrones, but with the
goodwill and co-operation of the lesser powers, who were, to be sure,
too feeble to resist her advance, but whose rights she was quite ready
to recognise, and even to promote, in her own way.
c10:p20.summary: The narrator notes that Lucilla builds her kingdom benevolently, with the cooperation of lesser powers, not by destroying existing hierarchies but by co-opting them.
c10:p20.best_quote: Thus Miss Marjoribanks prepared to establish her kingdom with a benevolence which was almost Utopian, not upon the ruins of other thrones, but with the goodwill and co-operation of the lesser powers

c2:p20.text:
She
knew, for example, that there was a great difference between the
brilliant society of London, or of Paris, which appears in books, where
women have generally the best of it, and can rule in their own right;
and even the very best society of a country town, where husbands are
very commonly unmanageable, and have a great deal more of their own way
in respect to the houses they will or will not go to, than is good for
that inferior branch of the human family.
c2:p20.summary: Lucilla understands that provincial society differs from metropolitan centers; in Carlingford, men control access to social spaces, so securing them through dining is the key to female influence.

c27:p57.text:
When Dr
Marjoribanks had gone downstairs to resume the case which he was writing
out for the  Lancet , Lucilla passed through one of those moments of
sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the
benefactors of their race. A few tears came to her eyes as she reflected
upon this great problem. Without such trials genius would not fully know
itself nor be justly aware of its own strength.
c27:p57.summary: Lucilla is moved to tears as she contemplates the problem of her unbelieving followers; without trials genius would not know its own strength.
c27:p57.best_quote: Lucilla passed through one of those moments of sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the benefactors of their race.

c18:p65.text:
While every one else regarded the matter with, to some extent, a
personal bias, the only person who looked at it abstractly, and
contemplated not the accidents of an evening, but the work itself, which
was progressing in the face of all kinds of social difficulties, was the
master-mind which first conceived the grand design of turning the
chaotic elements of society in Carlingford into one grand unity.
c18:p65.summary: While others gossip about personal interests, Lucilla alone views the evening abstractly, focused on the progress of her grand design to organize Carlingford society.
c18:p65.best_quote: While every one else regarded the matter with, to some extent, a personal bias, the only person who looked at it abstractly, and contemplated not the accidents of an evening, but the work itself, which was progressing in the face of all kinds of social difficulties, was the master-mind which first conceived the grand design of turning the chaotic elements of society in Carlingford into one grand unity.

c29:p45.text:
He had been doing without them
for a week or two, and he had not liked it; and yet at that moment it
seemed to Mr Cavendish that he could rather be content to lose them all
at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had
lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not,
after all, one of the Cavendishes, nor the person it took him for.
c29:p45.summary: Cavendish realizes he would rather be financially ruined than exposed as a fraud, revealing his desperate attachment to social position.
c29:p45.best_quote: he could rather be content to lose them all at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not, after all, one of the Cavendishes

c29:p68.text:
And then he went out
to discover, if possible, what was coming to him. The difference was,
that in this battle no honour, but only a possible salvage of reputation
and fortunate escape, was to be gained.
c29:p68.summary: Cavendish ventures out to face his crisis, understanding that he fights not for glory but for mere survival and the salvaging of his reputation.
c29:p68.best_quote: In this battle no honour, but only a possible salvage of reputation and fortunate escape, was to be gained.

c28:p78.text:
Lucilla regarded him through
all these fluctuations with natural pity, and at the same time with the
calmness of a knowledge which was aware of all and had nothing more to
discover; and at the end Mr Cavendish perceived her calm, and the
absence of wonder and curiosity in her face, and began to perceive that
he had something very serious to deal with—more serious even than he
had at first supposed.
c28:p78.summary: Lucilla watches Cavendish's emotional swings with calm knowing, while he gradually realizes the gravity of the situation.
c28:p78.best_quote: Lucilla regarded him through all these fluctuations with natural pity, and at the same time with the calmness of a knowledge which was aware of all and had nothing more to discover; and at the end Mr Cavendish perceived her calm, and the absence of wonder and curiosity in her face, and began to perceive that he had something very serious to deal with—more serious even than he had at first supposed.

c32:p22.text:
When he raised his
head and looked round him, naturally Mr Beverley's eyes went direct to
the mark like an arrow; he looked, and he saw at the centre of the
table, surrounded by every kind of regard and consideration, full in the
light of the lamp, his favourite adventurer, the impostor whom he had
denounced the first time he took his place by Miss Marjoribanks's side.
c32:p22.summary: The Archdeacon's eyes are drawn directly to Mr Cavendish, exposed fully in the lamp's light at the table's centre—the moment of revelation.
c32:p22.best_quote: he looked, and he saw at the centre of the table, surrounded by every kind of regard and consideration, full in the light of the lamp, his favourite adventurer, the impostor whom he had denounced

c33:p25.text:
"A criminal? a conspirator?" said Mr Cavendish, and he looked in his
accuser's face with an amazement which, notwithstanding his rage, struck
the Archdeacon. If he had called him an impostor, the culprit would have
quailed and made no reply. But the exaggeration saved him. After that
first look of surprise, he rose to his feet and confronted the avenger,
who saw he had made a blunder without knowing what it was.
c33:p25.summary: Cavendish reacts with genuine surprise to being accused of crime and conspiracy, revealing that the Archdeacon has made a strategic error by exaggerating the charges.
c33:p25.best_quote: A criminal? a conspirator? said Mr Cavendish, and he looked in his accuser's face with an amazement which, notwithstanding his rage, struck the Archdeacon.

c47:p28.text:
He
was there—he who had been so long away from Carlingford—he who had
been so deeply offended by hearing his name seriously coupled with that
of Barbara Lake—he who ought to have been anywhere in the world rather
than here upon the eve of his election, when all the world was keeping
watch over his conduct.
c47:p28.summary: Cavendish's presence in Barbara's parlour two days before the election represents a catastrophic breach of propriety and political judgment.
c47:p28.best_quote: He was there—he who had been so long away from Carlingford—he who had been so deeply offended by hearing his name seriously coupled with that of Barbara Lake—he who ought to have been anywhere in the world rather than here upon the eve of his election, when all the world was keeping watch over his conduct.

c47:p56.text:
When he was
coming out of the house, as a matter of course, he met with the chief of
his Dissenting supporters, accompanied (for Mr Bury, as has been said,
was very Low-Church, and loved, wherever he could do it, to work in
unison with his Dissenting brethren) by the Rector's churchwarden, both
of whom stopped with a curiously critical air to speak to the Candidate,
who had to be every man's friend for the time being.
c47:p56.summary: Cavendish encounters his key supporters leaving the Lake house, and their critical looks suggest they have observed and judged his visit.
c47:p56.best_quote: When he was coming out of the house, as a matter of course, he met with the chief of his Dissenting supporters, accompanied (for Mr Bury, as has been said, was very Low-Church, and loved, wherever he could do it, to work in unison with his Dissenting brethren) by the Rector's churchwarden, both of whom stopped with a curiously critical air to speak to the Candidate

c18:p50.text:
Whether it
was that little speech of hers which touched the mimic's heart, or
whether the effect was produced by some other secret influence, it is
certain that this was the night on which Mrs Woodburn's talent came to
what may be called a sort of apotheosis. She shook off her languor as by
a sudden inspiration, and gave such a sketch of the Archdeacon as up to
this day is remembered more clearly in Carlingford than the man himself.
c18:p50.summary: Mrs Woodburn suddenly recovers her powers and delivers a brilliant mimicry of the Archdeacon that becomes legendary in Carlingford.
c18:p50.best_quote: She shook off her languor as by a sudden inspiration, and gave such a sketch of the Archdeacon as up to this day is remembered more clearly in Carlingford than the man himself.

c25:p2.text:
The mimic was a little indolent, and would not take the trouble
to make any exertions for the good of the community, except in the
exercise of her peculiar talent, though she had been known, when
excited, to go through real fatigue for that; but she had none of the
steady force, the persevering energy—or, to sum up all in one word, the
genius—of Miss Marjoribanks, who, for her part, recognised the  use  of
such an instrument of entertainment as Mrs Woodburn possessed without
appreciating it in her own person; for Lucilla had no sense of humour,
as she candidly admitted, with that consciousness of her own faults, and
slight disposition to consider them virtues, which is common to persons
of great endowments.
c25:p2.summary: The narrator elaborates the fundamental difference: Mrs Woodburn relies on mimicry and entertainment talent, while Lucilla possesses steady organisational force, though Lucilla lacks humour despite her other gifts.
c25:p2.best_quote: Lucilla had no sense of humour, as she candidly admitted, with that consciousness of her own faults, and slight disposition to consider them virtues, which is common to persons of great endowments.

c7:p40.text:
Of course, there will be a party that will get
up a memorial, and prove that a man so kind-hearted never existed out of
paradise; and there will be another party who will prove him to be
insane; and then at the end all the blackguards within a hundred miles
will crowd into Carlingford, and the fellow will be hanged, as he
deserves to be; but I assure you it's a famous amusement for a country
town."
c7:p40.summary: The barrister elaborates that executions provide entertainment, with predictable memorials, insanity defences, and crowds of criminals attending.
c7:p40.best_quote: it's a famous amusement for a country town.

c18:p51.text:
She took him off to his very face, and he never found it out, though
everybody else did, and the house shook with restrained laughter.
c18:p51.summary: Mrs Woodburn's mimicry is performed in the Archdeacon's presence, but he remains completely unaware while the company laughs in barely restrained hilarity.
c18:p51.best_quote: She took him off to his very face, and he never found it out, though everybody else did, and the house shook with restrained laughter.

c18:p48.text:
Her
instinct, even when reason suggested that she should be doubtful of
them, was always to side with her own friends; and though there might be
persons included in that sacred number who were scarcely worthy of the
character, yet Lucilla, like every lofty character, could act but
according to her own nature, and could not forsake any one whom she
supposed to be thus mysteriously and darkly assailed.
c18:p48.summary: Lucilla's instinct is always to protect her friends, even against reason; her nature compels her loyalty regardless of their worthiness.
c18:p48.best_quote: Her instinct, even when reason suggested that she should be doubtful of them, was always to side with her own friends; and though there might be persons included in that sacred number who were scarcely worthy of the character, yet Lucilla, like every lofty character, could act but according to her own nature, and could not forsake any one whom she supposed to be thus mysteriously and darkly assailed.

c27:p59.text:
When Lucilla had shed
these few tears over her subjects' weakness and want of faith, she rose
up again in new strength from the momentary downfall. It was, as we have
said, a sublime moment. The idea of giving them up, and leaving their
affairs to their own guidance, never for an instant penetrated into her
heroic mind; but she was human, and naturally she felt the prick of
ingratitude.
c27:p59.summary: Lucilla rises from despair with renewed commitment to her causes; her heroism lies in persisting despite ingratitude.
c27:p59.best_quote: The idea of giving them up, and leaving their affairs to their own guidance, never for an instant penetrated into her heroic mind; but she was human, and naturally she felt the prick of ingratitude.

c36:p22.text:
People who know no better may go
away upon marriage tours, or they may fly off to foreign travel, or go
out as governesses, when all things do not go just as they wish. But as
for Miss Marjoribanks, she stood bravely at her post, and scorned to
flinch or run away. Thus commenced, amid mists of discouragement, and in
an entire absence of all that was calculated to stimulate and
exhilarate, the second grand period of Lucilla's life.
c36:p22.summary: While lesser people flee through marriage, travel, or governessing when disappointed, Lucilla stands firm at her post and begins her second campaign amid discouragement and without support.
c36:p22.best_quote: But as for Miss Marjoribanks, she stood bravely at her post, and scorned to flinch or run away. Thus commenced, amid mists of discouragement, and in an entire absence of all that was calculated to stimulate and exhilarate, the second grand period of Lucilla's life.

c46:p43.text:
She had
no vocation, such as the foundress of such an establishment ought to
have, nor did she see her way to the abandonment of all projects for
herself, and that utter devotion to the cause of humanity which would be
involved in it; but yet, when a woman happens to be full of energy and
spirit, and determined that whatever she may be she shall certainly not
be a nonentity, her position is one that demands thought.
c46:p43.summary: Lucilla lacks true religious vocation but will not surrender personal ambition; her energetic temperament creates an unresolved ethical dilemma.
c46:p43.best_quote: but yet, when a woman happens to be full of energy and spirit, and determined that whatever she may be she shall certainly not be a nonentity, her position is one that demands thought

c27:p65.text:
We mention this fact rather as a contribution to the
history of those phenomena of the human mind, which have as yet escaped
the metaphysician, than as an actual circumstance in the life of Miss
Marjoribanks. She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple,
unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla's heart
when she said "Poor Tom!"
c27:p65.summary: The narrator remarks that this psychological phenomenon—genius finding comfort in simple faith—is remarkable and deserves attention.
c27:p65.best_quote: She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple, unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla's heart when she said 'Poor Tom!'

c50:p10.text:
She even had the strength to get up to meet him, and hold
out her hands to him by way of welcome—but found herself, before she
knew how, in the arms of a man with a beard, who was so much changed in
his own person that he ventured to kiss her, which was a thing Tom
Marjoribanks, though her cousin, had never dared to do before.
c50:p10.summary: Lucilla rises to greet Tom but finds herself embraced by a bearded, transformed man who dares to kiss her.
c50:p10.best_quote: she found herself, before she knew how, in the arms of a man with a beard, who was so much changed in his own person that he ventured to kiss her, which was a thing Tom Marjoribanks, though her cousin, had never dared to do before.

c50:p23.text:
"Lucilla," said Tom Marjoribanks, "you know I always had a great regard
for my uncle. But it was not for him I came back. He was never half so
fond of me as I am of you. You know that as well as I do. There never
was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if
you had told me; and I have done it as near as possible.
c50:p23.summary: Tom declares his deep regard for Lucilla has always exceeded his regard for her father, and that he left for India at her behest.
c50:p23.best_quote: There never was a time that I would not have gone to the other end of the world if you had told me; and I have done it as near as possible.

c50:p18.text:
It was natural, and indeed it was only proper, that Miss Marjoribanks
should cry—which she did abundantly, partly for grief, and partly
because of the flutter of agitation, and something like joy, in which
she was, and which, considering that she had always frankly owned that
she was fond of Tom, was quite natural too.
c50:p18.summary: Lucilla cries abundantly, partly from grief over her father and partly from emotional agitation and unexpected joy at Tom's presence.
c50:p18.best_quote: partly for grief, and partly because of the flutter of agitation, and something like joy

c18:p47.text:
People who like to discover the alloy which blends
with all human motives, may suppose that Lucilla felt her own credit as
the leader of society at stake, and would not admit that she had been
duped. But this had in reality but a very small share in the matter.
c18:p47.summary: While others might suppose Lucilla's self-interest drives her actions, Oliphant asserts that reputation concerns play only a minor role in her character.
c18:p47.best_quote: People who like to discover the alloy which blends with all human motives, may suppose that Lucilla felt her own credit as the leader of society at stake, and would not admit that she had been duped. But this had in reality but a very small share in the matter.

c36:p1.text:
We have recorded her beginning in all the fulness of youthful confidence
and undaunted trust in her own resources; and have done our best to show
that in the course of organising society Miss Marjoribanks, like all
other benefactors of their kind, had many sacrifices to make, and had to
undergo the mortification of finding out that many of her most able
efforts turned to other people's profit and went directly against
herself.
c36:p1.summary: The narrator reviews Lucilla's initial confidence and early achievements in organizing Carlingford society, while noting the ironic cost of her efforts.
c36:p1.best_quote: like all other benefactors of their kind, had many sacrifices to make, and had to undergo the mortification of finding out that many of her most able efforts turned to other people's profit

c24:p85.text:
And it was not even the scriptural coals of fire she was
thinking of as she pondered her great undertaking in her mind. The
enterprise might not be free from a touch of human vanity, but it was
vanity of a loftier description: the pleasure of exercising a great
faculty, and the natural confidence of genius in its own powers.
c24:p85.summary: Lucilla's motivation is not even malicious revenge but rather a noble vanity—the pleasure of exercising her great talents and the confidence of genius in its own powers.
c24:p85.best_quote: And it was not even the scriptural coals of fire she was thinking of as she pondered her great undertaking in her mind. The enterprise might not be free from a touch of human vanity, but it was vanity of a loftier description: the pleasure of exercising a great faculty, and the natural confidence of genius in its own powers.
